Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Keep the supplied language.", "input": "At 7:40 on Tuesday, Lena Ortiz unlocked the rear workshop at Bell Street Printworks and began the scheduled ventilation check. The room held two screen-printing benches, a washout sink, and a small curing cabinet, with the extraction hood mounted above the ink table. The check was planned before the first production shift so the crew could use the room while the equipment was tested. Lena carried a calibrated vane meter, a smoke pencil, and the maintenance log from the office.

She first looked over the system without switching it on. A strip of blue tape on the hood marked the filter panel that had been opened the previous Friday. Its catches were seated, the gasket showed no tears, and no loose ink cloth had been left against the intake. Lena noted a light layer of paper dust on the ledge, but it had not reached the grille. She wiped the ledge and recorded the cleaning before moving to the fan isolator.

The fan started on the first attempt, though its sound was rougher than the steady hum recorded in the log two months earlier. Lena listened beside the motor housing and then at the duct bend above the drying rack. There was no repeated knock or scraping noise. A faint vibration came through the wall bracket, so she checked its two visible bolts with a spanner. Both were snug, and the bracket had no fresh marks where it met the wall.

At the hood, she held the vane meter in the center of each marked opening for a full minute. The readings varied slightly as the doors to the washout area moved, but settled when the room was still. She wrote down the average for the front, center, and rear positions rather than selecting the highest reading. The front position was the weakest. Lena repeated that measurement after checking that the meter's arrow faced into the airflow, and the second result was close to the first.

1. Hood and fan observations
   - Fan started normally and ran throughout the measurement period.
   - No obstruction was visible at the grille or in the accessible filter panel.
   - Airflow readings were recorded at three marked positions, with the front position lowest.
   - A small amount of vibration was felt at the wall bracket; its visible bolts were secure.

Lena next used the smoke pencil to see how air moved around the work surface. With the curing cabinet closed, the smoke traveled upward toward the hood from all three bench positions. At the front edge it drifted sideways before rising, which matched the lower meter reading. When the washout door stood open, a cross-draft pulled the smoke toward the corridor. Closing that door restored the upward path, so she entered the door position beside each set of observations.

The shop supervisor, Ben, came in while Lena was recording the second smoke test. He asked whether the fan had passed its check. Lena replied, “I’ve finished the measurements, but I haven’t compared them with the service limits yet.” Ben said the first shift was due in twenty minutes and moved the drying rack away from the hood. The rack had been parked closer than usual because a delivery pallet occupied its marked floor space.

Lena measured the distance from the rack to the hood and wrote it in the log, then repeated the center reading with the rack in its usual position. The value changed only slightly, while the smoke rose more cleanly from the rear bench. She photographed the original rack position and the clear working position with the shop tablet. The images showed the hood, floor marks, and rack wheels; no staff members were in the frame.

She also checked the make-up air grille near the entrance. Its face was clear, but a folded delivery sheet had been tucked under the lower edge of the grille cover. Lena removed the sheet and placed it with the paperwork on the supervisor’s desk. The grille cover remained secure, and she did not remove it because the check required only a visual inspection of its accessible face. The airflow at the hood was then measured once more with the corridor door shut.

Ben asked Lena to send the preliminary figures to the morning crew so they would know where to leave the rack. She said she would put the figures and the rack photograph in the maintenance log, but would not circulate the preliminary note to the crew until she had checked the service limits. The crew could still see the floor marks and keep the rack in its usual position. Ben acknowledged the distinction and returned to the press room.

Lena compared the readings with the limits printed on the equipment service sheet, using the range for the hood’s installed fan setting. She copied that range into her notes so a later reviewer could see which reference she had used. The front reading remained the lowest of the three, and the repeat measurements were consistent with the earlier set. She did not adjust the fan control or open the ductwork during this visit; those actions were outside the scheduled visual and airflow check.

Before leaving, she entered the time, instrument identification, room conditions, door positions, and rack location in the maintenance log. She attached the two photographs and filed the removed delivery sheet with the shop’s daily papers. The log showed the fan running, the repeated measurements, and the observed cross-draft when the washout door was open.
